name: Maca root

card.summary: An Andean root vegetable sold as a libido and energy supplement; a small number of trials suggest possible benefit for sexual desire, with limited evidence overall.
card.note: A systematic review described evidence as limited; a French agency warned about possible health risks of powdered root, which others dispute.

quick.overview:
Maca is a radish-like root grown at high altitude in the Peruvian Andes, eaten as food for centuries and now sold worldwide as powder, capsules and extracts. It is marketed for libido, energy and fertility.

A 2010 systematic review found four randomized trials, with two reporting improved sexual desire or function, one reporting an effect in men with erectile dysfunction and one finding no effect in cyclists; its authors called the evidence limited. A 2026 review reports improved libido in men-only and mixed-sex studies and inconsistent results in women.
quick.mechanism: The mechanism is not established. Maca does not appear to contain hormones; proposed actives include glucosinolates, macamides and alkaloids such as imidazoles, and Wikipedia notes that no pharmacokinetic data have been published.
quick.risks: Maca has a long record as food in the Andes. Wikipedia notes extracts contain MTCA, a compound that may act as an MAO inhibitor, and that France's food-safety agency warned consumers about powdered root, a concern others dispute on the grounds that boiling deactivates it.

lead: Maca (Lepidium meyenii) is a biennial plant of the cabbage family cultivated at 4,000 to 4,500 meters in the central Andes of Peru, grown for its fleshy hypocotyl-taproot [1][2]. Archaeological evidence shows cultivation around Lake Junín from about 1700 BC, and Spanish chroniclers described it in the early 1600s [1]. Commercial interest grew from the late 1980s, driven by its purported effect on fertility [1].

In supplement markets it is sold for libido, stamina and hormonal balance, and is a common ingredient in men's testosterone and sexual-health products [3][4]. Wikipedia describes research on its medicinal properties as inconclusive [1]. A 2010 systematic review concluded there is limited evidence for its effectiveness on sexual function [5].
infobox: Dried root, flour, gelatinized powder, extracts [1]

paras: Traditionally the root is roasted, boiled into porridge or juice, or fermented into a weak beer, and eaten in quantities exceeding 20 grams per day in Andean communities [1][2]. Supplement products use dried powder or concentrated extracts [1]. In looksmaxxing and men's-health contexts it is marketed for libido and energy; one DailyMed-listed product combines maca extract with tongkat ali and sea buckthorn [4].

A 2010 systematic review (Shin and colleagues) identified four randomized controlled trials: two reported positive effects on sexual desire or dysfunction, one found no effect in healthy cyclists and one reported significant effects in men with erectile dysfunction. The authors described limited evidence and called for more rigorous studies [5]. A 2016 systematic review is described by Wikipedia as suggesting improved semen quality, and a 2011 review found evidence for menopausal symptoms inconclusive [1].

A 2026 review reported that maca appeared to improve libido in studies of men and mixed-sex groups, that results in women (often postmenopausal) were inconsistent, and that most trials used about 3 g per day of powder; the author called for additional research [5].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists trials of maca in male sexual dysfunction, postmenopausal sexual function, antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction and exercise performance, several with very small samples [6].

Wikipedia notes that no pharmacokinetic data have been published and that maca extracts contain MTCA, which may act as a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and possible mutagen; France's food-safety agency warned consumers about powdered root, while others argued boiling deactivates MTCA [1].
Maca contains imidazole alkaloids, glucosinolates and macamides, as well as mostly carbohydrate dry matter [1][7].

Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa described maca about 1598; it was traded for lowland staples and used to pay Spanish colonial taxes [1]. Peruvian institutions accused Chinese companies in 2014 of illegally exporting maca and of biopiracy [1].
